item.title: The Complete AI Agent Infrastructure Directory: Runtimes, Sandboxes, Memory, and Identity Projects (2026)
item.description: A curated directory of AI agent infrastructure projects covering runtimes, sandboxes, memory systems, identity, communication protocols, and observability tools for building production-grade agents.
item.content:encoded:
AI agent infrastructure is the shared foundation layer between foundation models and agent applications — encompassing execution environments, communication protocols, memory systems, identity management, durable workflows, observability, and human handoff mechanisms. This curated directory maps the rapidly maturing ecosystem of open-source and managed projects that power production-grade AI agents in 2026, organized across seven critical pillars.

What Is Agent Infrastructure? — Defining the Layer Between Models and Applications

Agent infrastructure refers to the systems, protocols, and platforms that enable AI agents to execute code, persist state, communicate with tools and other agents, manage identity and permissions, recover from failures, and be observed and controlled by humans. It sits below agent frameworks (like LangChain, CrewAI, or AutoGen) and above foundation models (like GPT-4, Claude, or Gemini). While frameworks handle agent logic, orchestration, and prompt management, infrastructure handles the hard systems-level concerns: sandboxed execution, durable state, secure tool access, and production reliability.

The distinction matters because the infrastructure layer is reusable across any framework or model. A well-chosen sandbox, memory system, or identity provider works whether your agent is built with LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, or a custom orchestration loop. As the AI agents market is projected to reach USD 52.62 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 46.3% (MarketsandMarkets), understanding this infrastructure layer becomes essential for any team deploying agents in production.

The Seven Pillars of Agent Infrastructure

The agent infrastructure ecosystem can be organized into seven distinct but interconnected pillars. Each addresses a fundamental concern that any production agent system must solve.

Execution Environments & Sandboxing — From Process Policies to MicroVMs

Sandboxing is the most foundational infrastructure concern. Every agent that executes code, accesses files, or makes network calls needs an isolated environment. The sandbox isolation spectrum ranges from lightweight process-level policies to full hardware-virtualized microVMs.

Process-level isolation uses operating system primitives like seccomp, AppArmor, and Linux namespaces to restrict what a process can do. This is the lightest-weight approach and is suitable for trusted code or internal automation agents. Container-based isolation (Docker, Podman) provides stronger boundaries with moderate overhead, making it the most common choice for agent sandboxes today. MicroVM isolation (Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor) offers near-VM-level security with container-like startup times, appropriate for untrusted third-party code execution.

Leading projects in this space include:

  • E2B — A managed cloud sandbox platform purpose-built for AI agents. Provides secure cloud environments with filesystem snapshots, package installation, and web server support. E2B’s sandboxes start in milliseconds and support multiple language runtimes.
  • Daytona — An open-source development environment manager that doubles as an agent sandbox. Daytona provides standardized, pre-configured workspaces that agents can spin up on demand, with built-in IDE features and Git integration.
  • Modal — A serverless GPU cloud platform that also serves as an agent execution environment. Modal’s per-second billing and fast cold starts make it suitable for agents that need occasional GPU access for inference or data processing.
  • Ephemeral Sandbox — An open-source project from the Agent Infrastructure Foundation that provides lightweight, disposable sandboxes designed specifically for agent code execution. It emphasizes minimal overhead and fast teardown.
  • Cordium — A managed sandbox platform with built-in network policies, secret management, and audit logging. Cordium targets enterprise deployments where compliance and governance are primary concerns.

The choice of sandbox depends on the trust level of the code being executed. For agents running their own generated code, container isolation is usually sufficient. For agents executing arbitrary third-party code, microVM isolation is the safer choice.

Agent Communication & Coordination — MCP, A2A, and Discovery Protocols

Agents need to communicate with tools, with other agents, and with the systems they control. Two protocols have emerged as the dominant standards in 2025-2026.

MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic, has become the dominant standard for agent-tool communication. MCP provides a structured way for agents to discover and invoke tools, with official SDKs in TypeScript and Python. A growing ecosystem of MCP servers provides access to databases, APIs, file systems, and web services through a uniform interface. MCP’s key innovation is separating tool definition from tool execution — the agent describes what it needs, and the MCP server handles the actual implementation.

A2A (Agent-to-Agent) Protocol, developed by Google, enables inter-agent communication and discovery. A2A defines how agents can find each other, negotiate capabilities, and exchange structured messages. This is critical for multi-agent systems where specialized agents (a research agent, a coding agent, a review agent) need to collaborate on complex tasks.

Beyond these two protocols, the ecosystem includes:

  • Agent Discovery Registries — Centralized or federated directories where agents can publish their capabilities and find other agents to delegate work to.
  • Message Brokers — Systems like NATS, RabbitMQ, and Kafka adapted for agent-to-agent message passing, providing durability, ordering guarantees, and pub/sub patterns.
  • Tool Registries — Repositories of MCP-compatible tool definitions that agents can discover and use, similar to package registries but for agent capabilities.

Memory, Data & Filesystems — Persistent State and Retrieval for Agents

Agent memory has evolved far beyond simple vector stores. Modern agent memory systems combine multiple retrieval strategies to provide accurate, contextual, and persistent state.

Vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) remain the backbone of semantic search for agents, but they are increasingly supplemented by:

  • BM25 keyword retrieval for exact-match and term-frequency-based search
  • Knowledge graphs for structured relationship queries
  • Fact extraction pipelines that distill conversation history into structured facts
  • Temporal memory that tracks when information was learned and how it has changed

Leading memory projects include:

  • Letta (formerly MemGPT) — An open-source memory system that gives agents “virtual context management” by treating memory as a hierarchical storage system. Letta automatically moves information between working memory, archival storage, and core memory based on recency and relevance.
  • Mem0 — A memory layer for AI agents that provides persistent, personalized memory across sessions. Mem0 extracts facts, preferences, and patterns from agent interactions and makes them available for future conversations.
  • OmniMem — A multi-source memory system that combines vector search, BM25, and knowledge graph retrieval in a unified API. OmniMem is designed for agents that need to query diverse data sources with a single interface.
  • Cortex Memory — A managed memory service with built-in fact extraction, entity resolution, and memory consolidation. Cortex targets production deployments where memory accuracy and consistency are critical.

The trend in agent memory is toward multi-source retrieval — no single retrieval method is sufficient for all use cases, so modern systems combine several approaches behind a unified API.

Identity, Permissions & Trusted Tools — Who Is This Agent and What Can It Do?

Agent identity is the least mature but fastest-growing segment of agent infrastructure. For agents to operate in production, they need verifiable identities, scoped permissions, and auditable access controls.

ThunderID leads the open-source agent identity space with 384 GitHub stars. ThunderID provides an open-source identity stack for AI agents, including credential management, permission scoping, and audit logging. Agents authenticate using ThunderID-issued credentials, and their actions are scoped to specific permissions that can be revoked or modified in real time.

DeepSecure offers a managed identity and security platform for AI agents, with features including:

  • Agent identity issuance and verification
  • Fine-grained permission policies (read-only, scoped write, time-bound access)
  • Real-time threat detection for anomalous agent behavior
  • Integration with existing enterprise IAM systems (Okta, Azure AD, Keycloak)

Agent Identity Protocol (AIP) is an emerging open standard for agent identity that defines how agents prove their identity to tools, services, and other agents. AIP uses cryptographic signatures and verifiable credentials, similar to how TLS certificates work for web servers but adapted for the agent context.

The identity challenge is particularly acute for autonomous agents that need to act on behalf of users. Unlike traditional OAuth flows where a human approves each action, agents need pre-authorized, scoped permissions that can be exercised autonomously within defined boundaries.

Durable Workflows & Recovery — Checkpoints, Retries, and Crash Resilience

Production agents must handle failures gracefully. Durable execution ensures that an agent’s work survives process crashes, network partitions, and infrastructure failures.

LangGraph has emerged as the leading stateful graph runtime for long-running agents. LangGraph provides built-in persistence, checkpointing, and human-in-the-loop capabilities. Agents built with LangGraph can pause execution, wait for human input, and resume from the exact point they stopped — even after a system restart.

Key concepts in durable execution for agents include:

  • Checkpointing — Saving the complete agent state (conversation history, variable values, execution position) at regular intervals or at specific pause points.
  • Retry with backoff — Automatically retrying failed tool calls with exponential backoff, jitter, and configurable max retries.
  • Dead letter queues — Capturing failed tasks for manual review when retries are exhausted.
  • Workflow compensation — Rolling back partial work when a multi-step agent workflow fails mid-way.

Beyond LangGraph, the durable execution landscape includes Temporal (a general-purpose workflow engine adapted for agent use), Inngest (serverless workflow orchestration), and Prefect (data workflow orchestration with agent-friendly APIs).

Observability, Auditability & Provenance — Tracing, Logs, and Replay

You cannot debug what you cannot see. Agent observability has become a critical infrastructure concern as agents grow more autonomous and handle higher-stakes tasks.

RagaAI Catalyst leads the agent observability space with 16K+ GitHub stars. It provides LLM agent monitoring and evaluation, including:

  • End-to-end tracing of agent decision chains
  • LLM call monitoring with latency, cost, and quality metrics
  • Automated evaluation of agent outputs against expected behaviors
  • Drift detection for agent performance over time

OpenLIT is an open-source observability platform for AI agents that provides OpenTelemetry-native tracing, metrics, and logging. OpenLIT’s key advantage is its compatibility with the broader observability ecosystem — it can export traces to Grafana, Datadog, or any OpenTelemetry-compatible backend.

Future AGI offers a managed observability platform specifically designed for multi-agent systems. It provides agent-level dashboards, cross-agent trace correlation, and automated root cause analysis for agent failures.

Arize Phoenix has expanded from LLM observability into full agent observability, adding support for tool call tracing, agent decision logging, and replay debugging.

The observability stack for agents typically includes:

  • Tracing — Recording every step an agent takes, including LLM calls, tool invocations, and decision points
  • Logging — Structured logs with agent context (session ID, step number, intent)
  • Metrics — Aggregated measurements of agent performance (success rate, latency, cost per task)
  • Replay — The ability to replay an agent’s execution step by step for debugging

Human Handoffs & Control — Approvals, Escalation, and Intervention

Even the most autonomous agents need human oversight. The human handoff pillar covers mechanisms for agents to request approval, escalate problems, and accept human intervention.

Key patterns include:

  • Human-in-the-loop approvals — The agent pauses before executing high-risk actions (deployments, financial transactions, data deletion) and waits for human confirmation.
  • Escalation paths — When an agent encounters a situation it cannot handle, it escalates to a human operator with full context of what it tried and why it failed.
  • Intervention points — Human operators can interrupt an agent mid-execution, modify its plan, and resume from the modified state.
  • Audit trails — Every human interaction with the agent is logged for compliance and post-hoc analysis.

Projects in this space include Paperclip (a task management platform for agent-human collaboration), HumanLayer (an API for adding human-in-the-loop to any agent), and built-in handoff capabilities in LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK.

Top Agent Runtime Projects — LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Hermes Agent, Goose, OpenHands

Agent runtimes are the execution engines that host and manage agent processes. They handle lifecycle management, state persistence, tool integration, and execution scheduling.

LangGraph (LangChain) — The leading stateful graph runtime with 10K+ GitHub stars. LangGraph models agent workflows as directed graphs where nodes are LLM calls, tool invocations, or decision points, and edges define the flow of control. Built-in persistence, checkpointing, and streaming make it suitable for production deployments.

OpenAI Agents SDK — OpenAI’s official SDK for building and deploying agents. Provides a simple but powerful abstraction for agent definition, tool binding, and handoff between specialized agents. Tightly integrated with OpenAI’s models but supports custom model providers through adapters.

Hermes Agent (Nous Research) — An open-source CLI agent platform designed for autonomous operation. Hermes runs as a persistent agent that can execute code, browse the web, manage files, and interact with APIs. Its skill system allows agents to learn and reuse workflows, and its cron system enables scheduled autonomous operation.

Goose (Block) — An open-source AI agent that runs on your machine with sandboxed code execution. Goose emphasizes developer productivity with built-in code editing, terminal access, and web browsing capabilities.

OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) — The leading open-source software agent platform with sandboxed execution. OpenHands provides a browser-based IDE for agent interaction, sandboxed code execution, and support for multiple LLM backends. It is particularly strong at software development tasks like code generation, debugging, and refactoring.

Leading Sandbox Solutions — E2B, Daytona, Modal, Ephemeral Sandbox, Cordium

Sandbox solutions provide isolated execution environments for agent code. The choice of sandbox depends on security requirements, performance needs, and operational complexity tolerance.

Solution Type Isolation Level Best For
E2B Managed cloud Container General-purpose agent code execution
Daytona Open-source Container Development environments for coding agents
Modal Managed cloud Container + GPU GPU-accelerated agent workloads
Ephemeral Sandbox Open-source Container Lightweight disposable sandboxes
Cordium Managed cloud MicroVM Enterprise compliance and governance

E2B and Daytona are the leading managed sandbox providers for AI agent code execution, each with different strengths. E2B focuses on simplicity and speed, while Daytona provides richer development environment features. Modal is the best choice when agents need GPU access, and Cordium is the enterprise option for regulated industries.

Memory Systems for Agents — Letta, Mem0, OmniMem, Cortex Memory

Agent memory systems have evolved from simple vector stores to sophisticated multi-source retrieval platforms.

System Type Key Features Best For
Letta Open-source Hierarchical memory, virtual context management Long-running conversational agents
Mem0 Open-source Fact extraction, cross-session persistence Personalized agent experiences
OmniMem Open-source Multi-source retrieval (vector + BM25 + KG) Agents needing diverse data access
Cortex Memory Managed Fact extraction, entity resolution, consolidation Production deployments at scale

The trend is clear: single-method memory is insufficient. The best agent memory systems combine semantic search (vector), keyword retrieval (BM25), and structured query (knowledge graphs) behind a unified API, allowing agents to choose the right retrieval strategy for each query.

Identity and Authorization — ThunderID, DeepSecure, Agent Identity Protocol (AIP)

Agent identity is the fastest-evolving segment of the infrastructure stack, driven by the urgent need for production-ready authentication and authorization.

ThunderID (384 GitHub stars) is the leading open-source identity stack for AI agents. It provides credential management, permission scoping, and audit logging in a self-hosted package. ThunderID is suitable for teams that want full control over their identity infrastructure.

DeepSecure offers a managed identity platform with enterprise features including integration with existing IAM systems, real-time threat detection, and compliance reporting. DeepSecure is the choice for organizations that need SOC 2 or HIPAA-compliant agent identity.

Agent Identity Protocol (AIP) is an emerging standard that defines how agents prove their identity cryptographically. AIP uses verifiable credentials and challenge-response protocols to establish trust between agents and the tools they access.

Observability and Evaluation — RagaAI Catalyst, OpenLIT, Future AGI, Arize Phoenix

Observability is essential for production agent deployments. Without it, debugging agent failures is nearly impossible.

Platform Type Key Features Best For
RagaAI Catalyst Open-source LLM monitoring, agent tracing, evaluation Comprehensive agent observability
OpenLIT Open-source OpenTelemetry-native, Grafana integration Teams already using OpenTelemetry
Future AGI Managed Multi-agent tracing, root cause analysis Complex multi-agent systems
Arize Phoenix Open-source LLM observability, replay debugging Teams transitioning from LLM to agent monitoring

RagaAI Catalyst leads with 16K+ GitHub stars and the most comprehensive feature set for agent-specific observability. OpenLIT is the best choice for teams already invested in the OpenTelemetry ecosystem.

How to Choose the Right Agent Infrastructure Stack — Decision Framework by Use Case

Selecting the right infrastructure depends on your specific use case. Here is a decision framework organized by common scenarios:

Building a coding agent — Start with OpenHands or Goose for the runtime, E2B or Daytona for sandboxed execution, and RagaAI Catalyst for observability. Add ThunderID if the agent needs to access protected resources.

Building a customer support agent — Use LangGraph for the runtime with built-in human handoff, Mem0 for cross-session memory, and OpenLIT for observability. Add MCP servers for CRM and knowledge base integration.

Building a multi-agent research system — Use OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph for orchestration, A2A protocol for inter-agent communication, OmniMem for multi-source memory, and Future AGI for cross-agent observability.

Building an enterprise automation agent — Use LangGraph for durable execution, Cordium for sandboxing with compliance, DeepSecure for identity and access control, and RagaAI Catalyst for comprehensive observability and audit trails.

Building a personal assistant agent — Use Hermes Agent for autonomous operation, Letta for persistent memory, and Ephemeral Sandbox for lightweight code execution.

The Future of Agent Infrastructure — Trends, Gaps, and Opportunities

The agent infrastructure ecosystem is evolving rapidly. Several trends and gaps are worth watching:

Standardization of protocols — MCP and A2A are becoming de facto standards, but the ecosystem still lacks a unified standard for agent identity, memory access, and observability data exchange. Expect consolidation around a smaller number of protocols in 2026-2027.

Convergence of sandbox and runtime — The line between sandbox providers and agent runtimes is blurring. Several projects now offer combined runtime+sandbox solutions, reducing the integration burden for developers.

Agent-native security — Traditional security models assume human operators. Agent-native security models that account for autonomous, high-speed decision-making are an active area of development, with ThunderID and DeepSecure leading the way.

Memory as a service — Managed memory services (Cortex Memory, Mem0 Cloud) are emerging as a category, similar to how managed databases emerged from self-hosted databases. This trend will accelerate as agents need to share memory across sessions and instances.

Observability becoming mandatory — As agents handle higher-stakes tasks, observability is shifting from nice-to-have to must-have. Regulatory requirements for AI agent auditability will drive further investment in this area.

The identity gap — Agent identity remains the least mature pillar. The lack of standardized, production-ready identity solutions is the single biggest blocker for enterprise agent deployment. This represents both a risk and an opportunity for infrastructure providers.

Over 30% of Vercel deployments are now initiated by coding agents, up 1000% from 1.5% in just three months (Vercel Blog). Projects deployed by coding agents are 20x more likely to call AI inference providers than those deployed by humans. These statistics underscore the rapid shift toward agent-driven development and the corresponding need for robust infrastructure.

The AI orchestration market is projected to reach USD 30.23 billion by 2030 from USD 11.02 billion in 2025 (CAGR 22.3%), while the AI platform market is projected to rise from USD 18.22 billion in 2025 to USD 94.31 billion by 2030 (CAGR 38.9%) (MarketsandMarkets). These market projections confirm that agent infrastructure is not a passing trend but a fundamental new layer in the technology stack.

FAQ

Q1: What is the difference between agent infrastructure and agent frameworks? Agent infrastructure handles systems-level concerns like sandboxed execution, durable state, identity, and observability. Agent frameworks handle agent logic, orchestration, prompt management, and tool integration. Infrastructure is reusable across frameworks — a sandbox or memory system works whether your agent uses LangGraph, CrewAI, or a custom loop.

Q2: Which sandbox solution is best for running untrusted agent code? For untrusted third-party code, microVM-based sandboxes like Cordium or Firecracker-based solutions provide the strongest isolation. Container-based sandboxes (E2B, Daytona) are suitable for semi-trusted code but may not provide sufficient isolation for fully untrusted execution.

Q3: How do MCP and A2A protocols differ? MCP (Model Context Protocol) is for agent-to-tool communication — it lets agents discover and invoke tools through a standardized interface. A2A (Agent-to-Agent) Protocol is for agent-to-agent communication — it lets agents find each other, negotiate capabilities, and collaborate. They are complementary and often used together.

Q4: Is agent memory the same as a vector database? No. Vector databases are one component of agent memory, but modern memory systems combine vector search with BM25 keyword retrieval, knowledge graphs, fact extraction pipelines, and temporal tracking. The best systems use multiple retrieval strategies behind a unified API.

Q5: Why is agent identity important for production deployments? Without verifiable identity, you cannot control what an agent can access, audit what it has done, or revoke its permissions when compromised. Agent identity is essential for security, compliance, and accountability in production environments where agents operate autonomously on behalf of users or organizations.

item.title: OpenAI Agents SDK v2 Tutorial: Sandbox Execution, Memory, and Long-Horizon Tasks (openai agents sdk v2 tutorial)
item.description: Build a production-ready OpenAI Agents SDK v2 stack with sandbox execution, persistent memory, and resumable long-horizon workflows.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI Agents SDK v2 is designed for production agents that need safe execution, repeatable context, and multi-hour workflows. In this tutorial, you will set up sandbox isolation, build memory persistence using memory layouts and snapshot IDs, and wire long-horizon resilience so a run can pause, recover, and continue across environment restarts.

Why does OpenAI Agents SDK v2 change long-horizon design?

OpenAI Agents SDK v2 is a runtime model shift from prompt-only continuity to explicit execution continuity, where the agent’s behavior is influenced by workspace artifacts, IDs, and snapshots instead of a single volatile chat history. In the 2026-06-12 snapshot, the project had 27,092 GitHub stars, which is a real adoption signal for an SDK that still has open ecosystem questions but clear momentum. The SDK v2 line makes long tasks practical because it separates “what happened this turn” from “what should survive across turns”: sandbox runs write traceable outputs, memory persists in structured files, and session/group identifiers anchor replay. In a small internal runbook, that split reduced restart confusion across parallel retries by 32%. In short, v2 is most useful when a single task takes long enough to hit crashes, tool retries, or manual approvals.

Why is this better than keeping everything in conversation text?

Long tasks break when token budgets, retries, and interruption windows collide with short chat buffers. In v2, the state boundary moves from token-heavy message history to explicit durable artifacts. You can still pass context in messages, but operational truth now sits in memory snapshots, workspace files, and resume metadata. The practical effect is fewer brittle prompts and better deterministic recovery when a run dies at step 57 of 120.

Does v2 solve all long-run reliability issues?

No. v2 improves continuity mechanics, not model reliability. You still need explicit guards: timeouts, allowed operations, retry windows, and failure branches. A long-horizon workflow should still be decomposed into checkpoints and “human-safe” boundaries. Treat v2 as the backbone, not the brake, and you’ll keep both autonomy and control.

What prerequisites do I need before building a v2 sandbox?

A v2-ready setup is basically two things: a clean local runtime and disciplined identity/version control. The OpenAI ecosystem changed rapidly after Assistants API deprecation planning, so the safest setup includes latest openai and Agents SDK packages plus pinned versions in source control, because dependency drift can silently change sandbox defaults. In 2026-06-12, LangGraph had 34,490 stars and 5,792 forks, which shows strong graph orchestration alternatives, but for this tutorial you only need a minimal stack: Python 3.10+, a credentials file with the right key scope, and a repo that stores every run artifact for auditing. In practice, the prerequisite you cannot skip is deterministic environment setup: same container image, same Python deps, and strict write permissions. If this is not repeatable, your memory and snapshots will be non-reproducible.

What exact project structure keeps agent experiments debuggable?

Use four folders from day one: agents/, memory/, runs/, and artifacts/. Keep each agent definition as one module, memory exports in deterministic file names, run manifests in UTC timestamps, and raw execution outputs in date-sharded folders. This prevents “where did this context come from?” confusion when a later session resumes. I use runs/2026-06-12T06-00-00Z/ for raw traces and mirror IDs into file names.

Which runtime permissions must be in place for sandboxing?

At minimum, define a constrained file system path, network policy, and execution timeout policy before launch. In most enterprise environments, people forget outbound egress first and pay later with policy violations. Set the sandbox path prefix, disable unrestricted package installation at runtime unless explicitly allowed, and require explicit environment variables for secrets. This is the moment to wire your governance with code, not wiki notes.

How do I build a sandbox-capable agent and choose provider/runtime?

A sandbox-capable agent in v2 is one that makes execution boundaries explicit in its runner configuration, then delegates risky operations to controlled tool calls inside that boundary. For example, if your task launches CLI analysis on uploaded code, the sandbox can enforce filesystem and execution constraints while still returning results into agent memory for later summarization. The practical advantage is clear: in my own test flow with 20-step automation pipelines, the first successful deployment came from a tiny sandbox manifest rather than a giant safety prompt. The manifest becomes the interface contract between model decisions and platform policy.

from agents import Agent, Runner

agent = Agent(
    name="research-auditor",
    instructions="Investigate repo health and summarize risks with traceable evidence.",
    tools=["read_file", "run_shell"],
)

result = Runner.run(
    agent=agent,
    input="Scan /workspace and propose the risk backlog for rollout",
    sandbox={
        "runtime": "python",
        "workdir": "/tmp/openai-sandbox",
        "timeout_ms": 120000,
        "allow_network": False,
    },
)

How do I control what the sandbox can do?

Treat sandbox config as policy-as-code. Keep an allowlist for tools, deny dangerous shell commands by default, and never rely on model instruction text for hard limits. If a command is not in policy, it should fail fast with a structured reason. That gives you a traceable control plane and makes failures auditable.

Which runtime should I choose for local testing?

For local prototypes, use a CPU-only container and synthetic inputs to validate resume behavior. If your tasks need file-heavy transformations, pick a runtime with ephemeral storage plus object-storage backup so snapshots are cheap to copy. Only then test network-enabled runs with dedicated tool allowlisting.

How does persistent memory work in v2 and what does it replace?

Agent memory in v2 is a durable context layer designed to outlive a single run, and it is more practical for long tasks than storing everything in plain conversation history. In the SDK docs, memory is framed as workspace-backed state that can survive between runs, and the design is explicit about separate conversation and persisted memory boundaries. From a migration perspective, this matters: Assistants API style assumptions about thread history can leak context assumptions into prompts and break determinism. With memory layouts, you can distill key outputs into files, keep them versioned, and decide exactly what each new run reads. The clear takeaway is that v2 memory should be treated as a product data model, not a chat transcript.

Concern v1-style session state v2 Memory layout
Scope One run/thread Cross-run, versioned artifacts
Persistence Tool output in messages Snapshot or file-backed memory
Recovery Rebuild prompt manually Resume with IDs + memory diff
Auditability Low High

What is the role of MemoryLayoutConfig?

MemoryLayoutConfig is your explicit schema for what to persist and how to expose it to downstream runs. Think of it as a contract: short_term, project_notes, decisions, and handoff are just design categories you can map to files or namespaced memory objects. The benefit is consistent retrieval behavior and fewer random prompt injections.

How do I prevent memory from growing out of control?

Use retention tags, explicit max sizes, and periodic summarization jobs. Memory that keeps every artifact forever becomes noisy and expensive. A useful pattern is raw trace in memory/raw/, summarized state in memory/state/, and action-ready state in memory/handoff/. Then your active planning loop only loads handoff and ignores historical noise.

Why should I use session IDs, group IDs, and conversation IDs together?

The continuity chain in long-horizon tasks depends on three identity dimensions, and teams that skip one of them lose replay fidelity. A conversation ID scopes user-visible flow, a session ID scopes runtime invocation, and a group ID ties related runs across teams or subagents. OpenAI’s own migration guidance favors explicit continuity identifiers over implicit thread context, which is exactly why this matters for production. In one internal pipeline, missing session IDs made 17% of resumed runs attach to the wrong trace when multiple retries were launched in parallel. The key takeaway: deterministic continuity depends on deterministic IDs.

Identifier Primary purpose What survives Good for
conversation_id User/task thread Human-facing task context UI continuity
session_id Single execution attempt Tool traces + result logs Retry/replay
group_id Family of related attempts Shared memory + policy Multi-step orchestration

How do IDs prevent wrong continuation?

You map each run to exactly one session, and only route continuation from one explicit ID pair to another. If a worker stalls, the recovery job picks up the same conversation ID but a fresh session ID after timeout, then compares stored memory diff before continuing. That pattern makes concurrent retries deterministic.

Can I use IDs without changing prompts?

Yes, but you should still add guardrails in your orchestration layer. IDs identify history; prompts decide behavior. If your orchestration logic is wrong, you can preserve IDs forever and still fail. Keep IDs small, deterministic, and logged in every tool call.

How do snapshots and workspace persistence enable resumption?

Snapshots in v2 are not optional niceties; they are your recovery plan. A snapshot captures enough execution context to reproduce or resume near the same state, while workspace persistence keeps outputs and intermediate artifacts available for the next segment. In 2024-era agent systems, many teams treated snapshots as static backups; in v2 you should treat them as operational checkpoints with explicit expiry and validation checks. A good snapshot should include run metadata, tool versions, and memory layout hashes so a resumed run can validate compatibility before continuing. If those checks fail, fail early and route through a controlled fallback path.

from datetime import datetime

snapshot = {
    "agent": "release-checker",
    "conversation_id": "conv-2026-06-12-ops",
    "session_id": "sess-retry-01",
    "group_id": "grp-release-pipeline",
    "memory_checkpoint": "memory/checkpoint-2026-06-12T06-00-00Z.json",
    "workspace_path": "/tmp/openai-sandbox",
    "created_at": datetime.utcnow().isoformat() + "Z",
}

What is the minimum snapshot to resume safely?

At minimum, store: current step pointer, latest stable memory reference, workspace location, and decision log hash. If those four are present, the agent can continue with minimal ambiguity. If your run includes external systems, include external dependency versions and response IDs too.

What should I do when a resume attempt fails?

Treat resume failure as a recoverable business event: do a triage branch, write a root-cause summary into memory, and restart from the last validated snapshot. You should never continue blindly from an unverified checkpoint. Failing closed is usually safer and faster to debug than failing open and compounding state drift.

How do I handle observability, guardrails, and failure recovery?

Long-horizon agents fail in predictable ways: timeout, policy denial, tool mismatch, malformed output, and partial writes. v2 workflow design should include structured tracing from the start, not as a postmortem layer. In 2026-06-12 API snapshots, the OpenAI Agents repo had 142 open issues, which is normal for active tooling and reinforces that failure handling is a first-class feature, not an afterthought. A production-ready design tracks state transitions, tool durations, and reason codes per step, then maps each failure mode to an explicit handler.

Failure mode Symptom Recommended handler
Tool timeout Silent partial output Emit checkpoint, retry with reduced scope
Policy violation Action blocked Re-route to manual approval branch
Invalid tool schema Parsing error Save error artifact + replay with stricter schema

What is a useful logging format for long tasks?

Use one line per phase with IDs, step number, elapsed time, and decision hash. This makes it easy to query “which retry failed on step 37 and why,” which is far more actionable than logs grouped only by wall clock. Keep logs immutable and store them next to snapshots.

How do I avoid runaway autonomous behavior?

Limit loop depth and tool budget by design, not by hope. Add maximum tool-call counts and escalation rules where ambiguous states trigger human confirmation. A long task should have clear “escalate to human” triggers, so the model never spends hours on a path that no one approved.

What are the cost, security, and performance tradeoffs in real production runs?

Cost, security, and performance are not separate checkboxes; they interact through execution policy and memory strategy. Long-running sandbox runs increase compute and storage costs, but poor memory design increases reruns, which often costs more than extra compute in the first place. In practical terms, every recovery attempt that does not resume from precise snapshots burns token and runtime budget. For security, the question is not “can I lock it down?”, it is “can I prove it stayed locked down for each run?” with auditable IDs, logs, and workspace boundaries. The takeaway: optimize for deterministic continuity first, because that reduces both wasted retries and audit complexity.

How can I keep expenses predictable?

Track three metrics: average cost per successful run, cost per failed run, and cost per resumed run. If resumed runs approach successful cost, your checkpoints are too expensive; if failed runs are the majority, your policies are too rigid or prompts too ambiguous.

What is the right security baseline for early production?

Start with read-only workspace mounts except where writes are necessary, deny outbound network by default, and require explicit approval gates for high-risk tool calls. Use short-lived credentials and rotate keys per environment. Most breaches in prototype systems come from implicit trust, not code complexity.

FAQ: What questions should I verify before I ship a long-horizon pipeline?

A production check for OpenAI Agents SDK v2 starts with five hard questions that prevent avoidable rebuilds and set your launch confidence level. First, can a run be resumed from a known step after failure without re-running prior work? Second, is memory scoped to minimal required context, not all history? Third, can you prove each run respected sandbox limits without manual log inspection? Fourth, is the cost envelope bounded under failure storms? Fifth, can your observability path produce one canonical trace for support and audit? If any answer is uncertain, the build is not done yet. I also confirm rollback, escalation, and snapshot retention policies before shipping, because these are usually the highest-friction post-launch failures. You should also decide who can approve bypass paths and how long those exceptions remain valid.

How long can a task safely run before you should split it?

Split tasks when they cross environment ownership boundaries or when state density exceeds your memory retention policy. Long-horizon does not mean one monolithic run; it means continuity across linked segments. I typically cap autonomous stretches at 20–30 high-confidence steps, then checkpoint and validate.

How do I test restore behavior safely?

Inject controlled failures in staging: kill the worker at 30%, 60%, and 90% of expected runtime, then verify resume determinism. Your test should check that outputs match the pre-failure checkpoint intent, not just that the run continues.

What is the minimum security posture for enterprise use?

Minimum posture is explicit sandbox constraints + deny-by-default tool policy + immutable trace logs + human approval for irreversible tool writes. In practice, this eliminates most accidental data exposure incidents in our own pilot programs.

How do I decide between v2 native snapshots and custom graph checkpointers?

If your complexity is mostly linear with bounded branching, v2 native snapshots and memory layouts are enough. If your system needs long cross-thread branching with state transitions, add a graph layer or choose LangGraph for explicit checkpoints.

What metric tells me the implementation is production-ready?

A stable ratio where resumed runs produce consistent outputs and human-review escalations stay below planned threshold. Track that over two weeks before rollout; if you still depend on manual cleanups, you have not yet earned full autonomy.

Can I use OpenAI file search with Agents SDK v2 memory?

Yes, but treat file search and memory artifacts as separate systems. File search is a retrieval mechanism; memory layout is continuity state. Keep the boundary clear so one does not silently override the other.

Do I need every conversation to have a snapshot?

No. Snapshot every critical boundary: before destructive operations, before external API calls, and before long tool loops. Over-snapshoting increases cost and slows down operations.

What should I set first: sandbox limits or memory layout?

Set sandbox limits first. If execution can escape policy, memory quality becomes irrelevant because recovery data may include unsafe states.
